title: Cherry-pick, revert and reset
description: Deep dive into git cherry-pick, git revert, and git reset. Learn the differences between soft, mixed, and hard resets, when to use each command, and how to safely undo changes without losing work.

data.text: **Cherry-pick, revert, and reset** are Git's three primary tools for manipulating commit history. Each serves a distinct purpose: cherry-pick copies a commit to another branch, revert creates a new commit that undoes a previous one, and reset moves the branch pointer to a different commit. Senior engineers must know when to use each, how they affect shared history, and how to recover from mistakes.
The Three Undo Tools Overview

Git provides multiple ways to undo work because each situation demands a different approach. The wrong tool can cause data loss, break teammate branches, or create confusing history. Understanding the nuances of cherry-pick, revert, and reset is essential for safe history management.

items.title: git cherry-pick
pros: Applies specific commits to another branch
cons: Creates duplicate commits with different SHA-1s
Can cause conflicts if context differs
Rewrites branch history if applied to current branch
items.bestFor: Backporting fixes, applying selective changes across branches

items.title: git revert
pros: Creates an inverse commit (does not rewrite history)
cons: Does not remove the original commit
Can clutter history with many reverts
items.bestFor: Undoing public changes, safe undo on shared branches

items.title: git reset
pros: Cleanly removes commits from current branch
cons: Hard reset can permanently lose work
Requires force push to update remote
items.bestFor: Local cleanup, undoing uncommitted work, rebase preparation

data.text: git cherry-pick Deep Dive

Git cherry-pick takes one or more commits from one branch and applies them as new commits on the current branch. This is useful for backporting bug fixes to release branches or selectively applying changes without merging an entire feature branch.

data.title: Cherry-Pick a Single Commit
data.content: Applying a bug fix from main to a release branch
data.code:
# On the release branch
git checkout release/v1.2

# Find the commit hash from main
git log main --oneline
# Output:
# a1b2c3d Fix payment timeout error
# e4f5g6h Add user profile page
# ...

# Cherry-pick the fix
git cherry-pick a1b2c3d

# If conflicts occur, resolve them and continue
git cherry-pick --continue

# Or abort the cherry-pick
git cherry-pick --abort

data.title: Cherry-Pick Conflicts
data.text: Cherry-pick replays the commit changes on top of your current branch. If the surrounding code has changed, the patch may not apply cleanly. Conflicts are common when cherry-picking across divergent branches.

data.title: Cherry-Pick Multiple Commits
data.content: Applying a range of commits from another branch
data.code:
# Cherry-pick a range of commits (oldest first)
git cherry-pick a1b2c3d^..e4f5g6h

# Cherry-pick multiple non-consecutive commits
git cherry-pick a1b2c3d e4f5g6h i7j8k9l

# Cherry-pick and squash into one commit
git cherry-pick --squash a1b2c3d
git commit -m "chore: apply security fix from main"

data.text: git revert Deep Dive

Git revert creates a new commit that undoes the changes introduced by a previous commit. Unlike reset, revert does not remove the original commit—it adds an inverse commit. This makes revert safe for public branches where rewriting history would break teammates.

data.title: Revert a Single Commit
data.content: Undoing a faulty commit safely on a shared branch
data.code:
# Find the commit to revert
git log --oneline
# a1b2c3d feat(auth): add OAuth2 login
# e4f5g6h fix(api): correct timeout handling

# Revert it (creates a new commit)
git revert a1b2c3d

# Git opens an editor for the revert commit message:
# Revert "feat(auth): add OAuth2 login"
# This reverts commit a1b2c3d.

# Push safely—no force needed
git push origin main

data.title: Revert a Merge Commit
data.content: Reverting a merge requires specifying which parent to revert to
data.code:
# A merge commit has two parents. Revert to the first parent (mainline):

git revert -m 1 a1b2c3d

# -m 1 means 'use the first parent as the mainline'
# This undoes the merge but keeps the branch history intact

# For a complex revert of multiple commits:
git revert --no-commit a1b2c3d e4f5g6h
git commit -m "revert: undo auth feature and api timeout fix"

data.title: Revert Merge vs Reset Merge
data.text: If you accidentally merged a bad PR, revert is safer than reset. Reset would require force-pushing and would break anyone who pulled the merge. Revert adds a new commit that undoes the changes, preserving history.
git reset Deep Dive

Git reset moves the current branch pointer to a specified commit, optionally updating the staging area and working directory. It has three modes: soft (moves branch, keeps changes staged), mixed (moves branch, unstages changes), and hard (moves branch, discards all changes).

data.title: git reset Modes Comparison
data.code:
# Assume HEAD is at C3, and you want to go back to C1
#
#   C1 --- C2 --- C3 (HEAD -> main)
#

# Soft reset: HEAD moves to C1, changes stay staged
git reset --soft C1
#   C1 (HEAD -> main) --- C2 --- C3 (staged)

# Mixed reset (default): HEAD moves to C1, changes unstaged
git reset C1  # or --mixed C1
#   C1 (HEAD -> main) --- C2 --- C3 (unstaged in working directory)

# Hard reset: HEAD moves to C1, all changes lost
git reset --hard C1
#   C1 (HEAD -> main)
#   (C2 and C3 are gone from this branch—but still in reflog!)

data.title: Hard Reset Destroys Work
data.text: git reset --hard permanently discards uncommitted changes and removes commits from the branch. Before using --hard, ensure your work is either committed or stashed. Use git reflog to recover if you make a mistake.

data.text: Understanding git reflog

Git reflog is the safety net for almost every destructive operation. It records every movement of HEAD and branch references. Even if you hard reset or delete a branch, reflog can recover the commits if they are still within the reflog expiration period (default: 90 days).

data.title: Reading git reflog
data.content: Inspecting and using reflog to recover lost commits
data.code:
# View reflog for HEAD
git reflog

# Output:
# a1b2c3d HEAD@{0}: checkout: moving from feature to main
# e4f5g6h HEAD@{1}: commit: add user profile
# i7j8k9l HEAD@{2}: rebase -i (finish): returning to refs/heads/main
# ...

# Recover a lost commit by resetting to its reflog entry
git reset --hard HEAD@{2}

# View reflog for a specific branch
git reflog show feature/old-branch

# Show when a specific commit was last referenced
git reflog | grep a1b2c3d

data.title: Recovering After git reset --hard
data.text: If you accidentally run git reset --hard, immediately run git reflog to find the previous HEAD position. Then run git reset --hard HEAD@{1} to restore. The 90-day reflog window gives you plenty of time to recover.
Resetting vs Reverting: When to Choose What

The choice between reset and revert depends entirely on whether the branch is shared. On a local branch with no collaborators, reset is fast and clean. On a shared branch, revert is safe because it does not rewrite public history.

data.title: Reset vs Revert Decision Guide
items: **Local branch, unpushed commits**: Use reset --soft or --mixed to clean up before pushing
**Local branch, pushed commits**: Use revert to avoid force-pushing
**Shared branch, your own commits**: Use revert unless you coordinate with the team
**Shared branch, someone else's commits**: Always use revert
**Accidental merge**: Use revert -m 1, not reset
**Rebase gone wrong**: Use reflog to find the original HEAD

data.title: Exercise: Undo Scenario Practice
data.description: Practice choosing the right undo tool for common Git emergencies.
steps: Scenario 1: You committed sensitive credentials to main. Fix with revert (safe) or reset (requires force push coordination).
Scenario 2: You rebased interactively and lost 3 commits. Fix with git reflog.
Scenario 3: A teammate merged a broken feature. Fix with git revert on main.
Scenario 4: You made 5 messy commits on a feature branch. Fix with git reset --soft HEAD~5, then recommit cleanly.
Scenario 5: You cherry-picked a commit to the wrong branch. Fix with git reset --hard HEAD~1 on that branch.
data.expectedOutcome: You can correctly identify the tool for each scenario and execute the commands safely.

data.text: Cherry-Pick Advanced Techniques

Cherry-pick has several advanced options for complex workflows. The --squash option applies changes without creating a commit. The -x option appends a cherry-pick reference to the commit message. The --onto option allows cherry-picking to a completely different branch.

data.title: Cherry-Pick with Squash
data.content: Applying changes without creating a new commit
data.code:
# Apply changes from a commit but stage them without committing
git cherry-pick --squash a1b2c3d

# Resolve any conflicts, then:
git add .
git commit -m "feat: backport user profile improvements to release"

# Benefits:
# - Clean single commit on target branch
# - Original commit message can be rewritten
# - No duplicate commit hashes in history

data.title: Cherry-Pick to Different Branch
data.content: Using --onto to cherry-pick to a branch other than HEAD
data.code:
# Cherry-pick from main onto a feature branch without switching HEAD
git cherry-pick --onto feature/dashboard a1b2c3d^ a1b2c3d

# Syntax: git cherry-pick --onto <target-branch> <upstream> <commit>
# This applies commit a1b2c3d to feature/dashboard

data.text: Revert Advanced Techniques
Reverting multiple commits, reverting merges, and creating revert commits without automatically committing are advanced scenarios that require specific flags.

data.title: Revert Multiple Commits at Once
data.content: Undoing a series of commits in a single revert commit
data.code:
# Revert multiple commits without committing each one
git revert --no-commit a1b2c3d e4f5g6h i7j8k9l

git commit -m "revert: undo auth refactor and api timeout changes"

# This creates ONE revert commit instead of three

data.title: Revert a Range of Commits
data.content: Undoing all commits in a range
data.code:
# Revert everything from HEAD~10 to HEAD~5 (6 commits)
git revert --no-commit HEAD~10..HEAD~5
git commit -m "revert: undo commits from last sprint"

data.text: Reset Advanced Techniques
Reset interacts with the staging area, working directory, and branch pointer. Understanding exactly what changes at each level is crucial for avoiding data loss.

data.title: Reset Mode Cheat Sheet
items: git reset --soft HEAD~1: Undo last commit, keep all changes staged
git reset HEAD~1 (mixed): Undo last commit, keep changes unstaged
git reset --hard HEAD~1: Undo last commit, discard all changes
git reset --hard origin/main: Force local main to match remote
git reset --hard HEAD: Discard all uncommitted changes (dangerous)

data.title: Squashing Commits with Reset
data.content: Combining multiple commits into one using reset --soft
data.code:
# You have 4 messy commits and want to combine them
git reset --soft HEAD~4

# All changes from the 4 commits are now staged
git commit -m "feat(auth): implement complete OAuth2 login flow"

# Result: one clean commit instead of four

data.title: Reset and Force Push
data.text: After a reset, your local branch has diverged from the remote. You must force push. Use --force-with-lease to prevent overwriting your teammates' work. Never force push to main without team coordination.
Working with Stash and Undo
The git stash is another safety net. If you need to undo uncommitted work temporarily, stash it. You can apply or pop the stash later. Stashes are also recorded in reflog.

data.title: Stash as a Safety Net
data.code:
# Before a risky operation, stash everything
git stash push -m "backup before reset"

# Perform the reset
git reset --hard HEAD~3

# If you need the work back:
git stash list
# stash@{0}: backup before reset

git stash pop stash@{0}

# Stash also appears in reflog:
git reflog | grep stash

data.text: Recovering from Common Mistakes
Every senior engineer has made Git mistakes. The difference between panic and confidence is knowing the recovery commands. Here are the most common mistakes and their fixes.

data.title: Common Git Mistakes and Fixes
items: **Accidentally committed to main**: git reset --soft HEAD~1, then git checkout -b feature/xxx, git commit, git push -u origin feature/xxx
**Force pushed and lost commits**: git reflog, find the lost commit, git reset --hard <reflog-hash>
**Merged wrong branch**: git reset --hard HEAD~1, then merge the correct branch
**Cherry-pick conflict abandoned**: git cherry-pick --abort returns to original state
**Reset --hard on wrong branch**: git reflog on that branch, find previous HEAD, reset back
**Deleted a branch with unmerged work**: git reflog, find the branch tip, git branch <name> <hash>

data.title: Exercise: Recovery Drills
data.description: Set up a test repository and practice recovering from each mistake scenario. Time yourself—senior engineers recover in under 60 seconds.
steps: Create a test repo with 5-10 commits
Practice each recovery scenario from the list above
Use git reflog to verify recovery
Measure your recovery time for each scenario
Write the commands in a personal cheat sheet

data.text: Understanding Git's Object Model

To truly master undo operations, you must understand Git's object model: blobs (file content), trees (directories), commits (snapshots with metadata), and tags (named references). Every undo operation manipulates these objects.

data.title: Git Objects and Undo
items: **Blob**: Immutable file content. Never deleted by undo operations (only by gc).
**Tree**: Directory structure. Rebuilt when commits change.
**Commit**: Immutable snapshot. Reset moves the branch pointer; commits still exist until gc.
**Tag**: Named reference to a commit. Deleted tags can be recovered via reflog if recently deleted.
**Ref**: Branch or tag name pointing to a commit. Reset and branch operations manipulate refs.

data.title: Garbage Collection
data.text: Git's garbage collector (git gc) removes unreachable objects. Commits that are no longer referenced by any branch, tag, or reflog entry become eligible for deletion. The default reflog expiration is 90 days, giving you a long window to recover.

data.text: Best Practices for History Management

data.title: History Management Rules
items: Never reset or rebase a branch that others are working on
Prefer revert over reset on shared branches
Use cherry-pick for selective backports, not for entire features
Keep feature branches short to minimize the need for complex history operations
Write descriptive commit messages so cherry-picked commits are self-explanatory
Use git reflog as your first response to any 'lost work' panic
Configure git config --global rerere.enabled true to auto-resolve repeated conflicts

items.text: Verified the branch is local (not shared) before using reset
items.hint: Run git branch -vv to see tracking status

items.text: Created a backup branch before destructive operations
Checked reflog after any operation that felt wrong
items.hint: git reflog immediately, do not make more changes

items.text: Communicated before force-pushing to shared branches
items.hint: Post in team chat: 'Force pushing main to fix commit order'

data.text: Advanced Scenarios
Real-world Git workflows often involve combinations of these tools. Understanding how cherry-pick, revert, and reset interact with rebase, merge, and stash makes you a more confident Git user.

data.title: Recovering from a Bad Rebase
data.content: Using reflog to recover after a rebase conflict disaster
data.code:
# You ran: git rebase main
# Conflicts everywhere. You resolved some, then accidentally aborted
# or lost commits. Here's the recovery:

# Step 1: Check reflog for the pre-rebase HEAD
git reflog
# abc1234 HEAD@{0}: rebase -i (finish): returning to refs/heads/feature
# def5678 HEAD@{1}: rebase -i (start): checkout main
# 1234567 HEAD@{2}: commit: add user profile (original position)

# Step 2: Reset to the original position
git reset --hard HEAD@{2}

# Your branch is back to where it was before the rebase.
# Now you can retry the rebase more carefully.

items.question: What is the difference between git reset and git revert?
items.answer: git reset moves the branch pointer backward, removing commits from the branch history. git revert creates new commits that undo the changes. Reset rewrites history; revert adds to it. Use reset for local cleanup, revert for public branches.

items.question: Can I undo a git reset --hard?
items.answer: Yes, if the commits were recent. Run git reflog to find the previous HEAD, then git reset --hard HEAD@{1}. If reflog has expired (default 90 days), recovery is much harder.

items.question: Does cherry-pick copy the commit author?
items.answer: Yes. cherry-pick preserves the original author and date. The new commit has a different SHA-1 hash because it has a different parent and timestamp, but the author is unchanged.

items.question: What happens if I cherry-pick a commit that is already in the branch?
items.answer: Git will say 'commit X is already up to date' and skip it. The commit is not duplicated. If you force it with --allow-empty, it creates an empty commit.

items.question: How do I revert a revert?
items.answer: Reverting a revert re-applies the original changes. Find the revert commit hash with git log, then run git revert <revert-commit-hash>. This creates a third commit in the chain.

items.question: Is git reset --soft the same as git commit --amend?
items.answer: Similar but not identical. --soft HEAD~1 undoes the last commit but keeps all changes staged. --amend replaces the last commit with new staged changes. Use --soft when you want to reorder or split commits.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Cherry-pick applies specific commits to another branch—useful for backports
Revert creates an inverse commit—safe for shared branches
Reset moves the branch pointer—fast but rewrites history
Hard reset discards work; soft reset keeps it staged
Reflog is your safety net for almost every mistake
Never reset or rebase branches that others are using
data.takeaway: Mastering cherry-pick, revert, and reset gives you surgical control over Git history. Use revert for safety, reset for cleanup, and cherry-pick for selective application.
